title: ETFs, Size, and the Commodity Problem - Systematic Investor 340

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/ETFs, Size, and the Commodity Problem - Systematic Investor 340.docx

summary: Top Traders Unplugged, March 2025: Fed projections and German fiscal shift, Mar-a-Lago accord and dollar risk, trend-following state, Global Investment Returns Yearbook, Quantica paper on trend-following capacity in commodities and ETF drag.

coverage.note: Tariffs, German debt brake, current account effects
Global yield spillovers, euro, FX vol, German fund size
Miran paper, Plaza Accord, Mar-a-Lago accord design
Dollar risks, Bretton Woods, 2008 dollar, commodity super cycles
Trend barometer, CTA sector P&L, transition periods
CTA/equity index numbers; introduction to yearbook
Drawdowns, pension assumptions, bond real returns
2020-24 macro drivers; trend best 5 years; intro to Quantica paper
Correlation, capacity cost, ETF drag, fees and size
Cost of size, crisis alpha from commodities, replicators

completeness_estimate: 0.89 - first reader was thorough on the Fed, Germany, dollar, Yearbook and Quantica capacity material; missed secondary points (defence spending leakage, Alan's verdict on a Mar-a-Lago accord, short- vs long-term trend at reversals, real vs nominal growth in 2020-24, five-year look-back method, sponsor bias caveat).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the FED has uh reduced its expectation for GDP this year and next year and um and increase its expectation for inflation so kind of there's a stagflationary bias
claims.claim: The March 2025 Fed projections cut GDP and raised inflation, showing a stagflationary bias even though the dots still imply two cuts.
claims.testable: partly - SEP data are public, mapping to returns is judgement

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the risk to growth are very much on the downside so they're all kind of almost all participants see greater downside risk to growth
claims.claim: The FOMC projections' diffusion indices show nearly all participants see downside risk to growth, the most negative since late 2022/2023, and upside risk to unemployment.
claims.indicator: FOMC diffusion index of risks to growth and unemployment

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they see the upside risk to inflation as as a high as it was um you know back when we had the inflation Spike
claims.claim: The inflation-risk diffusion index is as elevated as in 2021-22, so the Fed sees upside inflation risk as high as at the inflation spike.
claims.indicator: FOMC diffusion index of risks to inflation

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: clearly the risks are for more of a stag deflationary environment if they actually come through
claims.claim: Tariffs create stagflation-like risk (slower growth, higher inflation); outcome depends on how long tariffs last and in what shape.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: unwinding of the constraint of the debt break in Germany either committing to 500 billion Euro infrastructure uh fund and effectively unlimited um defense spending
claims.claim: Germany's debt-brake reform (EUR 500bn infrastructure fund, defence outside the spending limit) is a radical fiscal stimulus that changes the German growth outlook, with Bundesbank 0% growth forecasts likely revised to as much as 2%.
claims.direction: German growth up, German defence stocks and bund yields up

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: will mean less savings from from Europe being exported to the US so it's going to mean a um it's going to be a lower current account Surplus in Germany
claims.claim: Higher German spending reduces European savings exported to the US, lowering Germany's current account surplus and capital inflow to the US, partly addressing the US external deficit.
claims.indicator: German current account surplus; capital flows to US
claims.testable: partly - current account and TIC data

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: by pushing up German yields that's raising that's that means globally there's less excess savings so bond yields globally will be higher
claims.claim: German fiscal expansion and higher Bund yields reduce global excess savings, so bond yields globally (including US Treasuries) rise at the margin.
claims.direction: global yields up, US bonds down

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: probably also means a higher Euro over time as well
claims.claim: Stronger European growth and fiscal action should lift the euro over time.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you would think those two forces together would would lead to maybe less uh demand for us treasuries
claims.claim: Rising German/European yields combined with decades-high Japanese yields reduce foreign demand for US Treasuries, pushing US yields higher.
claims.indicator: Japan and German 10-year yields vs Treasuries

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: pick up in in volatility in the currency space uh where actually for Trend followers currencies haven't been a great uh sector for many years could lead to some interesting um opportunities
claims.claim: Major shifts in global yield and capital flows should raise FX volatility, creating opportunities for trend followers after years of weak currency-sector returns.
claims.testable: partly - testable via CTA FX sector returns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the infrastructure fund is 500 billion uh euros and German GDP is you know it's about 5 trillion might be a bit more bit less um so that's 10%
claims.claim: The EUR 500bn fund is about 10% of German GDP, so spread over ten years it adds about 1% of GDP per year before defence spending and multiplier effects.
claims.conditions: Depends on how much spending leaks abroad

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the ticker has lost investors two-thirds of their money
claims.claim: A leveraged single-stock ETF (2x Tesla, short Ford) lost two-thirds in five weeks, showing the risk of financially engineered ETF products.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a little bit too much Financial engineering going on in that ETF space
claims.claim: ETF wrappers allow almost any strategy to be packaged, including trend following, raising concern about financial engineering.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: on the one hand they want a weaker dollar to try and boost manufacturing that's been key I suppose uh
claims.claim: The US faces a dollar trilemma: a weaker dollar helps manufacturing, a stable dollar preserves reserve-currency status, and the huge deficits need enough stable capital inflows to be funded.
claims.conditions: Goals conflict so policy may shift

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: assuming Trump used tars primarily as a negotiating tool
claims.claim: Miran's paper treats tariffs primarily as a negotiating tool and part of a package to correct dollar overvaluation, which has hurt manufacturing via the trade deficit.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the plaza Accord was in 1985 between the US and its major trading partners that was an agreement to bring down the dollar um after a period of dollar uh overvaluation
claims.claim: The 1985 Plaza Accord is the precedent for a coordinated agreement to weaken the dollar after overvaluation, now dubbed a Mar-a-Lago Accord.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you are part of uh the US's security umbrella then that that what comes with that would be uh the benefit of security but you have to effectively pay for that somehow either buying treasuries
claims.claim: Proposals link the US security umbrella to FX and trade policy, requiring partners to pay by buying Treasuries or swapping holdings into century or perpetual bonds.
claims.indicator: foreign Treasury holdings swap into long bonds
claims.direction: longer Treasury duration held by foreigners

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: a lot of the uh a lot of the uh us treasuries are held by China the Middle East Japan
claims.claim: Treasury holdings are concentrated in China, the Middle East and Japan rather than European reserve holders, limiting how far a European-led accord could reduce the dollar.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: foreigners hold about 60 trillion in in in us assets and that's a function of the fact that the US has run deficits for years
claims.claim: Foreigners hold about $60T of US assets because of persistent US deficits, so any tampering with the dollar risks foreigners exiting and a disorderly dollar decline.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they have to supply dollars to the rest of the world and then they end up with a current account deficit and um and foreigners end up having large claims on the US
claims.claim: The Bretton Woods design makes the dollar the core reserve asset, so the US must supply dollars through current account deficits, leaving foreigners with large claims (a Triffin-type flaw).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the dollar got stronger during the the the uh financial crisis because there was so much debt issuance in dollars people had to scramble to buy dollars to be able to uh fund liability
claims.claim: Despite fears of a dollar collapse before 2008, the dollar rose in the crisis because dollar-denominated liabilities forced a scramble for dollars.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: usually these commodity super cycle which a lot of people have been expecting uh would you know take off anytime soon actually they often come with a change in the monetary system
claims.claim: Per Adam Rozencwajg, commodity super cycles often coincide with a change in the monetary system, so a shift in the dollar regime would support commodities.
claims.indicator: commodity super cycles; monetary regime change
claims.conditions: Requires a real monetary regime change

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own Trend barometer finished at 43 yesterday that's kind of neutral
claims.claim: The trend barometer (a measure of trend-model signal strength) at 43 is neutral, and CTAs had a six-week challenging period with a recovery in recent days.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: what's been causing um a fair bit of the pain has been in the currency sector
claims.claim: Trend followers' March 2025 pain came from currency reversals such as the sudden euro rebound, plus US equity sell-offs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we are long by definition when markets are making all-time highs and then when they turn uh it takes a while for for these position positions to be reduced
claims.claim: Trend followers are structurally long equities at all-time highs, so sell-offs produce giveback until models cut exposure, a lag inherent to trend following.
claims.conditions: At market turns, correction vs reversal
claims.testable: yes - lag measurable in CTA returns

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: has come from the commodity sector things like Metals uh in particular the precious metals have been really great supported by copper
claims.claim: Best trend-following returns in early 2025 came from precious metals, copper, live cattle, and shorts in JGBs and German bonds.
claims.indicator: CTA sector P&L: metals, livestock, short JGB/Bund
claims.direction: long metals, cattle; short JGB, Bund

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it's one of those transition periods that tends to be chopped be and difficult for Trend following obviously when the S&P is you know down 10% and after a prolonged upswing
claims.claim: After a prolonged equity upswing, a 10% S&P decline is a transition phase that is choppy and hard for trend following, the point in the cycle where it is most challenged.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: S&P 500 certainly uh the worst of them all down 4.6% uh for March and down 3.22% so far this year
claims.claim: As of mid-March 2025 the SG Trend index was down about 4% YTD, CTA index down 2.14%, short-term traders up, S&P 500 down 3.2%, global equities flat, aggregate bonds up 2.4%.
claims.indicator: SG CTA index, SG Trend, short-term traders, S&P 500 YTD

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it's really interesting to kind of look at it to help anchor I think long-term return expectations
claims.claim: Long-run return databases such as the Global Investment Returns Yearbook provide anchors for long-term asset return expectations.
claims.indicator: Global Investment Returns Yearbook (Marsh, Staunton, Dimson)

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the the the US Stock Market was uh largely uh driven by the performance of the the the the railways
claims.claim: Index composition changes dramatically over decades (railways about 60% in 1900, energy about 30% in the 1970s, financials 25-30% in 2007), so today's dominance of technology is unlikely to persist for 20 years.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the index have actually become much less cyclical like the cyclical um you know the financials energy those sectors have become a lot less uh uh dominant
claims.claim: The US index has become less cyclical as financials and energy shrank and technology grew, so cross-period valuation comparisons need adjustment.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: comfortably very comfortably uh you know outpacing bonds 4.6% and bills three 3.4% and in real terms at 6.6% in the US
claims.claim: Over 125 years US equities returned about 9.7% nominal (6.6% real) versus bonds 4.6% and bills 3.4% nominal, with the rest of world equity about 4.3% real, supporting US exceptionalism.
claims.indicator: US equity, bond and bill returns 1900-2024

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the market fell 79% in real terms you know uh huge draw down and how long did it take to come back out of it you know reached reclaimed the highs was 15 and a half years
claims.claim: Equity drawdowns can be deep and long: the Depression fell 79% in real terms and took 15.5 years to recover, so buy-and-hold has a worst case that matters near retirement.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: what makes so many Pension funds use much higher kind of expected returns for their portfolios and why do they own 80% of bonds in Europe
claims.claim: Pension funds assume expected returns far above long-run real bond returns (US real about 1.6%) while holding large bond allocations, an apparent inconsistency.
claims.indicator: long-run real bond returns vs pension return assumptions

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: across 21 different markets the average real return over the long term was 0.9% in bonds
claims.claim: Across 21 markets the long-run real bond return was only 0.9%.
claims.indicator: average real bond return in 21 countries

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: huge uh regulatory um you know forces uh kind of encouraging people to lock in bond yields to doe risk pensions
claims.claim: Regulation pushed pension funds to lock in bond yields to de-risk through the 2000s, helping push yields down and creating fragilities like the UK LDI crisis.
claims.direction: bond yields lower then forced selling

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: really does stand out as as a as a really negative down over 30%
claims.claim: In the long histogram of annual returns, 2022 bonds were down over 30% (real), a standout loss, while equity annual returns are skewed with 10-20% most frequent.
claims.indicator: annual bond and equity return distributions

correction.issue: Adds 'real' to the 2022 bond loss; the speaker only says down over 30% (and hedges with 'I think').
correction.fix: In the long histogram of annual bond returns, 2022 stands out as a loss of over 30% (speaker unsure of the figure), while annual equity returns are skewed with 10-20% the most frequent outcome.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: 73 74 was down 56% Tech bubble the same Global financial crisis uh Global financial crisis 52% it only took 5.3 years though to come back
claims.claim: Equity drawdowns were 56% in 1973-74, similar in the tech bubble, and 52% in the GFC (5.3 years to recover); the worst case wait for equities is 16 years in real terms.
claims.indicator: US equity drawdown and recovery time

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: draw Downs in equities have also been in you know of of much longer length actually than what you typically see uh in in the CTA space
claims.claim: Equity drawdowns last longer than typical CTA drawdowns, countering the common criticism that trend following drawdowns are long.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: so worst case scenario historically has been 16 years if it went immediately into draw then you would get your money back in real terms uh but actually in bonds it was 80 years
claims.claim: Worst-case recovery from a drawdown in real terms was 16 years for US equities but 80 years for bonds.
claims.indicator: time to recover in real terms

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: how persistently positive bonds and equities were up to you know what you know the 90s and now has turned positive again
claims.claim: Stock-bond correlation was persistently positive until the 1990s, turned negative from the late 1990s to the 2000s, an outlier period, and is positive again.
claims.direction: bonds fail to hedge equities when correlation positive

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you're kind of coming up with an inflation forecast over the next five years 3% is probably a better estimate I would guess
claims.claim: US inflation averaged 2.9% over 129 years vs 2.1% for Switzerland, so a 3% base rate is a better five-year forecast than the Fed's 2% target.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: anybody who locked in yields in uh 2020 at 0.5% or whatever in the US is going to get that nominal return which will prove to be very negative
claims.claim: Bond holders and pensions that locked in 2020 yields near 0.5% will earn very negative real returns after the inflation shock.
claims.indicator: bond yields locked in at 2020 lows

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you know momentum is very well placed in in those uh in those charts
claims.claim: In the Yearbook factor data by decade, momentum is the top-performing factor in both the US and UK, consistent with trend following belief.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: us equities uh did the S&P did 14.5% annualize so well above the you know uh just under 10% annualized which would be kind of your Baseline expectation
claims.claim: The S&P returned 14.5% annualised over 2020-24, versus a baseline of just under 10%, following two other favourable five-year periods (best 15-year run since 1970 per Bridgewater), helped by 2009 valuations and liquidity.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: just because it was it it proved to be the right decision uh or proved to be the best outcome doesn't mean it was the right decision not to diversify away from Equity
claims.claim: Resulting (Annie Duke): a good outcome does not prove a good decision, so strong equity returns do not show that not diversifying was right.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: real rates in the US have been negative over that whole five period fiveyear period on average so you've had negative real rates quantitive easing in the early part of it enormous fiscal simulus
claims.claim: Over 2020-24 average US real rates were negative, with QE and large fiscal deficits (about 8% of GDP), boosting nominal GDP via higher inflation (4.2% average) at 2.5% real growth, which explains the strong equity returns.
claims.indicator: real rates; fiscal deficit; nominal GDP
claims.conditions: Negative real rates plus fiscal stimulus

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Last 5 Years was the best for the stain Trend uh going back to 2005 performance was higher back then but the volatility of the index was much higher back then
claims.claim: On a volatility-adjusted basis the SG Trend index had its best five-year period since 2005, even though pessimism about trend following in 2019 would have predicted otherwise.
claims.indicator: SG Trend index 5-year return per unit vol

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Commodities are driven by more unique stories supply and demand stories
claims.claim: Commodities respond to idiosyncratic supply-demand drivers, so trend following in commodities has lower correlation to financial markets and is the main diversifier in a trend portfolio.
claims.indicator: correlation of commodity trend returns with financial trend returns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: when accessing uh commodity markets there are constraints because liquidity is not great
claims.claim: Commodity liquidity limits the assets a CTA can deploy, creating a tension between capturing commodity diversification and growing AUM.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the top 10 most liquid commodity markets account for 70% of the total liquidity in commodities
claims.claim: Of 69 commodity markets, the top 10 hold 70% of liquidity and are energy-heavy (WTI, Brent), so capacity-constrained programs lean on energy rather than diversifying agriculturals.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the expected sharp of that Trend following is twice that of the same strategy just applied on the top 10 most liquid strategies liquid Market
claims.claim: Quantica estimates trend following on all 69 commodity markets without capacity limits has twice the expected Sharpe of the same strategy on only the top 10 most liquid markets.
claims.indicator: trend following Sharpe, 69 vs top-10 commodity markets

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: much lower when you bring in cocoa and zinc and all of these smaller markets as opposed to if you're just looking at um WTI Brent gas oil gasoline
claims.claim: Average correlation is lower when small markets such as cocoa and zinc are included, versus energy contracts that are derivatives of the same market, explaining the Sharpe gain from breadth.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they estimate that there's about a 177% reduction in the sharp ratio because of that
claims.claim: For a $3-4bn trend program with about $1bn in commodities, capacity limits reduce the Sharpe (the transcript says 177%, likely 17.7%, about 0.16), so the sweet spot may be below $3-4bn or even below $1bn.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the expected structural drag on performance can be as high as 4% per year before fees
claims.claim: Trend-following ETFs trade only a fraction of markets, with structural drag up to 4% per year before fees (measured on commodities), which can outweigh their low-fee advantage.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when you offer a flat fee product uh or an ETF with a really low management fee only the only way you can really make it a profitable business is to go for size
claims.claim: Low-fee replication ETFs must scale to be profitable, which forces fewer, more liquid markets and hurts diversification, so size has a performance cost.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there is a cost to size and the cost is less diversification in terms of the Commodities
claims.claim: Size limits commodity diversification, which may also reduce crisis alpha when clients need it most.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's all the Commodities except for a couple of fixed income markets
claims.claim: In 2025 trend-following gains came from commodities and a few bond shorts, not from equities or currencies, so capacity-constrained commodity exposure reduces returns in such periods.
claims.indicator: source of CTA P&L in equity sell-off

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's actually around infliction periods that the correlation between the replicators and the benchmarks break down
claims.claim: Trend replicators diverge from their benchmark around inflection points, exactly the critical periods.
claims.indicator: correlation of replicators with CTA benchmark

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Trend followers did really well in 2008 and most of it actually came from Commodities
claims.claim: In 2008 trend followers did very well and most of the gain came from commodities.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you might expect the most liquid Commodities I'm talking energy oil and gold and copper and those kinds of markets to be most sensitive to economic conditions
claims.claim: Liquid commodities (oil, gold, copper) are most sensitive to economic conditions, so crisis alpha may come from them rather than from illiquid softs; this is unverified.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you only traded gold oil copper um nck gas and corn you're going to be more Diversified than if you trade five energies and they're more liquid
claims.claim: A smaller set of diversifying markets can beat a larger set of correlated ones, so how risk is allocated matters more than market count.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you could trade 20 markets and based on an on an average sharp of 0.2 and and an average correlation of 0.05 you get a sharp of 64 which could be way better than uh trading 100 markets
claims.claim: Portfolio Sharpe depends on the average Sharpe and average correlation: 20 markets with Sharpe 0.2 and correlation 0.05 yield about 0.64 (transcript says 64), potentially better than 100 more correlated markets.
claims.indicator: portfolio Sharpe formula (average Sharpe, average correlation)

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Trend falling programs that aim to trade hundreds of markets while managing billions of dollars in assets will likely experience a risk distribution that deviates from the theoretical optimal risk equal risk allocation approach
claims.claim: Programs trading hundreds of markets with billions in AUM deviate from equal-risk allocation, and many markets add more to marketing narrative than to risk or performance; Niels has never seen data showing hundreds of markets beat 70.
claims.indicator: number of markets in trend programs

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen read the Quantica quote about hundreds of markets and said he had never seen data supporting it, not Alan Dunne.
correction.fix: Speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (quoting Quantica). Programs trading hundreds of markets with billions in AUM deviate from equal-risk allocation, and many markets add more to the marketing narrative than to risk or performance; Niels has never seen data showing hundreds of markets beat about 70.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it remains to be seen one how much seeps set overseas and two you know normally in in a traditional kind of Keynesian perspective there's a multiplier effect
claims.claim: The growth impact of German defence spending depends on how much of it leaks abroad as imports versus going to domestic producers, plus an uncertain Keynesian multiplier; a broadened definition of defence (cyber, security) widens the domestic channel.
claims.indicator: domestic content of defence spending; fiscal multiplier
claims.direction: German growth up, less if spending leaks overseas
claims.conditions: depends on import share of defence procurement
claims.testable: partly - multipliers and import shares can be estimated but with wide error

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I don't think uh the solution being proposed by Steve Moran and this piece are de sttion largely because you know I don't think they necessarily work for for Europe or for for China
claims.claim: A Mar-a-Lago-style accord (partners selling dollars and terming out Treasuries) is unlikely because it does not suit Europe or China and US leverage over them is doubtful; unilateral Fed money-printing to buy foreign currency could spiral into something dangerous.
claims.direction: low odds of coordinated dollar devaluation
claims.conditions: Europe already moving to self-reliance on defence

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it has been kind of a six week uh or so uh challenging period for um Trend followers in particular um not so much the short-term managers
claims.claim: In choppy reversal periods, short-term trend traders hold up better than longer-term trend followers (in March 2025 the short-term traders index was up while SG Trend was down about 4% YTD).
claims.indicator: SG Short-Term Traders index vs SG Trend index
claims.direction: short-term trend outperforms long-term trend at reversals
claims.conditions: sharp trend reversals after long trends
claims.testable: yes - compare short- vs long-horizon trend returns around reversals

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: what we're seeing now in like in the UK is there's this push to encourage Pension funds to go into private market so you wonder well how's that
claims.claim: Regulators have a record of pushing pension funds into allocations that later misfire (2000s bond lock-in, LDI), so the current UK push into private markets deserves scepticism.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it only took 5.3 years though to come back so I mean maybe that's what keeps uh people well to come back and but people have to remember it took also a while to get into that draw down
claims.claim: Recovery time after the trough understates the full pain of an equity drawdown, because the slide into the trough also takes years; recent quick recoveries (GFC 5.3 years) may lull investors.
claims.indicator: drawdown duration (peak to trough plus trough to recovery)
claims.testable: yes - drawdown durations from return histories

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I think five years is a good period and we've just kind of halfway through the decade so it's interesting to look at that
claims.claim: Five-year look-backs are a useful complement to century-long data because they are recent enough to remember the starting consensus, showing how fast the macro regime can change (secular stagnation in 2019 to 4.2% inflation in 2020-24).
claims.indicator: rolling five-year asset and macro outcomes
claims.testable: partly - one can compare forecasts made at the start of each five-year window with outcomes

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: us real GDP averaged 2 and a half% which is the about the same as the previous five-year periods
claims.claim: US real GDP growth in 2020-24 (about 2.5%) was no better than prior five-year periods, so the exceptional equity returns came from nominal growth, deficits and negative real rates rather than superior real growth.
claims.indicator: US real GDP growth vs nominal GDP growth
claims.testable: yes - decompose returns into real growth, inflation and valuation

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I'm sure if we read some research from some of the um providers who run hundreds of of markets they would have compelling evidence as to why that's a good thing
claims.claim: Manager research on design questions (number of markets, capacity) tends to support the author's own business model, so findings should be weighed against the sponsor's incentives.
